```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)
```

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Background

Cross country and track are the two main running sports that comprise most of the calendar year for competitive runners, from high school through college and even the professional level. In cross country, runners trek through long distance races over sprawling courses. In track, there is a wide variety of races runners may participate in, from short sprints to many laps around the oval. Cross country occurs during the fall, while track occurs during the winter, spring, and into summer. Unlike sports such as basketball or volleyball, which are most often conducted in controlled environments, the sport of running is highly variable. The courses on which races are held can be very different from each other even if the distances are largely the same. Performance can be highly impacted by weather, conditions, location, time of the season, race stakes, and many other factors. 
  
  This project seeks to examine these outside factors and their influence on U.S. collegiate club running performance in particular. At major institutions, the sport of running generally falls within two levels: the varsity scholarship level and the club running level. The National Intercollegiate Running Club Association (NIRCA) is the main governing body of collegiate running clubs across the United States. These running clubs exist outside the NCAA and varsity scholarship athletics, allowing all runners the opportunity to compete and enjoy the sport. Member athletes can compete in club-sponsored races hosted across the country. They may also participate in regional races where they can compete against NCAA athletes. NIRCA encompasses both club cross country and club track, covering a wide range of races and distances.

### 1.2 Motivation

The tracking of statistics related to running performance is relatively new; whereas statistics have always been at the forefront of athlete analysis in major sports such as football and basketball, it is relatively recently that race data has begun to be seen as a useful tool for understanding the variability that comes with the sport. Online tools such as *Athletic.net* and *TFFRS* were founded in the 2000s to be able to host race results. However, these sites tend to only contain very basic results data: runner name, year, team, placement, overall time, and sometimes the average pace per mile. Thus, it can be hard to put into context the performances of the athletes.

  There exist some papers written within the past few years years that examine influencing factors on race-day performance, mainly focused on weather parameters. Many of these papers focus on the marathon distance; for instance, Knechtle et. al (2019) specifically looked at years of Boston Marathon results to determine the relationship between weather conditions, sex, country of origin, and running performance. Another paper by Mantzios et al. (2022) looked into the implications of temperature, humidity, and wind speed on performance in endurance running events across the globe, finding that heat has a particularly strong impact on reducing peak running abilities. While these papers determine some conditions that considerably impact running performance, they are mostly limited to very long distances (10K, marathons, etc.) and tend to focus mostly on weather variables only. Furthermore, these athletes tend to be professional runners and older. It should be noted that marathon athletes and races make up only a fraction of the sport.

  Researchers at Notre Dame, the founders of the dataset we seek to work with, wrote one of the first papers to use a publicly available running dataset that expands scope beyond the marathon. Their paper looks to provide an evidence-based framework on ideal race scheduling at the collegiate level based on athlete improvement trends throughout racing season (Karr, Fryer, et al., 2026). However, their research questions center around the athletes themselves, focusing on their improvement within a season and across multiple seasons. With our project, we hope to specifically examine the outside factors available in this dataset that contribute to the race environment and ultimately influence athlete performance, from weather and topography to race stakes. Our research will fill in some gaps identified earlier, including looking at a wider range of race types and focusing attention on a range of collegiate athletes rather than only professional runners and road racers. Furthermore, we will include track events into our study, which has not been a focus of previous reports. In this way, our findings become more relevant to a wider group of runners; it can provide valuable information on which "uncontrollable" factors impact race day the most so athletes can be best prepared to handle them.
    
### 1.3 Research Questions 
  
The following research questions center around factors that surround races, going beyond variables inherent to the athletes themselves:
  
- Do certain weather conditions impact performances across various race lengths differently? If so, how, and to what extent?
- How do race and training locations, particularly differences in altitude and topography, affect athlete performance? 
- Do the stakes of the race (regional, national, NIRCA-only, NCAA-hosted, early season/late season, etc.) push athletes to perform better?  



## 2. Data

### 2.1 Data Background and Sources
  
This investigation analyzes the public National Running Club Database (NRCD), archived on Zenodo (Karr, Darden, et al., 2026). The NRCD was originally founded and built by researchers at the University of Notre Dame, led by creator Jonathan A. Karr Jr., to give collegiate club runners the shared results infrastructure that NCAA Division I programs have historically enjoyed. Prior to the NRCD, public running data was heavily restricted, scattered across private spreadsheets or PDFs, or limited to small-scale studies without public downloadable datasets. The reliability and trustworthiness of the NRCD stem from its unique, moderated data collection pipeline. Unlike unverified web scrapes, results are submitted by club athletes and administrators, and then carefully reviewed and approved by moderators before entering the official corpus.


### 2.2 General Data Description

This project uses the `joined.csv` file from the NRCD dataset. The dataset is very large containing 180,767 rows (observations) and 70 columns (variables). The variables in this dataset encompass a wide variety of race factors, ranging from athlete details (gender, grade, team_name, result_time) to race and environment details (meet_city, altitude, event_type, and 21 variables that relate to aspects of the weather, such as wind and temperature). ID variables (result_id, meet_id, sport_id) give each result and event type a unique numerical identifier, while binary variables (regionals, nationals) identify the stakes of the race. From environmental factors to standardized times and venue data across many entries, this sampling of variables gives a glimpse into the breadth of the dataset.  
  
This dataset is useful to answer our research questions because it provides us with a wealth of information that goes beyond the race itself, from weather conditions to location and meet details that our research questions will require. The specificity of variables within this set will help us quantify trends and narrow down exactly which factors impact running performance. While traditional public tools like *Athletic.net*, *TFRRS*, and NCAA sites generally only report on basic variables such as runner names, teams, placements, and overall times without contextual depth, our data set has 70 different variables to consider. It includes crucial metrics ranging from exact runner start and end times to situational parameters like altitude, event types, temperatures, humidity, and wind. Because of this depth, we have the ability to look deeper into what affects performance.  


## 3. Exploratory Data Analysis

### 3.1 Data Cleaning

The initial dataset contained results from the main collegiate running sports of cross country and track. The stated goal of this study is to look into performance data surrounding the sports of cross country and track; therefore, initial phase of our data cleaning process centered around excluding entries for non-running track events, relay results, and road races from the analytical dataset. Standard naming conventions of running events, typically a numerical distance followed by a unit of length such as "5000m", were used to distinguish eligible running events from other athletic competitions. Furthermore, the last 11 columns were excluded from our analysis since they do not pertain to our stated goals. This leaves 59 available variables and around 160,000 observations.

```{r include=FALSE}
getwd()
list.files()

run = read.csv('joined.csv')
dim(run)
```

```{r include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(knitr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidytext)
library(lubridate)

# First, exclude all non-running events, relay races, and road races

trues = str_detect(run$event_name, '(\\d{2,5}m)|(Mile)') &
        !str_detect(run$event_name, 'x')

only_run = run[trues, ]
dim(only_run)
  
```

```{r include=FALSE}
# Next, grab only columns that could pertain to research questions
# Exclude relay columns, racewalk columns, road races

only_run = only_run %>% 
  select(1:59) %>%
  filter(sport_name != "Road Race")
dim(only_run)
```

#### Duplication Cleanup

This dataset includes over 21,000 rows where the result_ids are duplicated. As a part of the cleaning process, we investigated these rows to determine which ones were exact duplicates. There were 1,653 exact duplicate entries, which left us with 20,297 rows that had duplicate `result_id` numbers but were not exact duplicate rows. Initial findings saw that these rows tend to have slight negligible differences in weather measurements, potentially due to multiple weather recordings at a race or track meet. Otherwise, these rows seemed to contain the same result for a unique athlete. 

To prove this finding, we utilized a pipeline that filtered to duplicate result ID's; summarizing on the ID variables `athlete_id` and `meet_id` helped determine if each duplicated result id had a one-to-one relationship with the athlete and meet. We also used `result_time` to solidify whether these rows contained the same exact result, since the times more strongly identify a unique performance down to the second. Finally, using `count` returned a one-row result indicating that all duplicated result ID's correspond with one unique athlete and result. Thus, we concluded there is a high likelihood these are redundant. We made the decision to accept the first recorded entry for each duplicated result ID, since weather parameters are unlikely to change dramatically in the relatively small amount of race time.

After filtering out all duplicate entries, we are left with ~128,000 observations.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Filter out exact duplicate entries

only_run = only_run %>% distinct()
dim(only_run)

# Are remaining duplicate result_ids nearly the same?

dp = only_run %>%
  group_by(result_id) %>%
  filter(n() > 1) %>%
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    athletes = n_distinct(athlete_id),
    times = n_distinct(result_time),
    meets = n_distinct(meet_id),
  ) %>%
  count(athletes, times, meets)

dp

only_run = only_run %>% distinct(result_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
dim(only_run)
```

#### Handling Missing Weather Data

For key variables, which include ID variables, location, race classification, race distance, gender, and result time, there is rarely missing data. However, weather and climate variables experience more missing data; according to Karr, Fryer, et al. (2026), "meets from August 2023 onward carry comprehensive course distance, elevation gain and loss, weather at race time, and track venue metadata." Data on meets prior to this have much more limited information on weather, and indoor track meets will, of course, not have weather data present. 

Weather variables contain substantial missing data, making it necessary to evaluate their completeness before analysis. Temperature, humidity, and wind speed each have 64.61% missing observations in the cleaned dataset. Other variables, including precipitation (96.32% missing), snow measurements (100%), and UV index (100%), have considerably less available information. Therefore, temperature, humidity, and wind speed were selected as the primary weather variables for our analysis. It was also decided that a boolean variable `weather_true` would be created to help filter on entries that include data; this way, the original data is preserved, while weather analysis can simply filter on this new variable.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Show that temperature is always present for every entry with weather
# Should return zero rows since it is always present with other weather
only_run %>%
  filter(is.na(temperature) & !is.na(humidity)) %>%
  nrow()

# Create new variable to filter on
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(weather_true = !is.na(temperature))
```

Weather availability also differs by sport. Approximately 49.71% of cross country results and 21.50% of outdoor track results contain temperature measurements, while indoor track results have no recorded temperature data. Rather than removing observations without weather measurements from the entire dataset, we retained them for other research questions and created a separate subset for outdoor weather analysis. This preserves useful performance data while ensuring that weather comparisons use observations with the necessary environmental measurements.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run %>%
  group_by(sport_name) %>%
  summarise(
    total_results = n(),
    weather_results = sum(weather_true),
    weather_percent = round(mean(weather_true) * 100, 2)
  )
```

#### Gender Column Merge

For gender, we have two separate columns, `gender` which only was filled about half of the entries, and `gender_1` which was full. First, compared the entries of the two columns to ensure that none of them were different. This first `all` returns TRUE which tells us we do not have differences in rows where both columns are filled. Thus, we can combine them into one `gender` column for future analysis. 

```{r include=FALSE}
all(only_run$gender[!is.na(only_run$gender) & is.na(only_run$gender_1)] ==
    only_run$gender_1[!is.na(only_run$gender) & is.na(only_run$gender_1)])

only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(gender = gender_1) %>%
  select(-gender_1)

sum(is.na(only_run$gender))
only_run %>%
  count(gender)
```

#### Date Column Merge

There are multiple date columns in this dataset; we determined we could merge into one full `date` variable that has all of the start dates in them, since the small range of dates for each meet/race is not going to affect the racers times. We found that the variables `start_date` and `end_date` contained no missing values, while `date_of_event` missing many values. In finding the difference in days of the start date and end date, we find that only ~3% of entries had a different start and end dates, indicating meets occurred on a single day. Thus, we chose the `start_date` column to be the one date column.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(start_date = ymd(start_date), end_date   = ymd(end_date))

diff_days = abs(as.numeric(only_run$start_date - only_run$end_date))

summary(diff_days)
sum(diff_days > 1, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(diff_days > 2, na.rm = TRUE)

only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(date = start_date) %>%
  select(-start_date, -end_date, -date_of_event)
```

#### Race Time Conversion and Performance Standardization

Race finishing times were originally stored as character values in different formats depending on event length. Shorter races were typically recorded in seconds, while longer races were recorded in minutes or hours. To ensure consistency across events, we added a column converting result times into seconds. This transformation allows us to perform numerical calculations and compare results across different race distances. The original finishing times were preserved, while a new variable, `time_seconds`, was created to store the converted numerical values. This conversion also provides the foundation for standardizing performance across different events.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    time_add = case_when(
      str_count(result_time, ":") == 0 ~ paste0("0:0:", result_time),
      str_count(result_time, ":") == 1 ~ paste0("0:", result_time),
    ),
    time_seconds = as.numeric(hms(time_add))
  ) %>%
  select(-time_add)
```

Because raw finishing times cannot be directly compared across different race distances, we standardized finishing times within each combination of sport, event, and gender. This accounts for differences in typical finishing times between race types and between men's and women's competitions. Standardized times represent how far an individual result falls above or below the average finishing time for comparable performances, measured in standard deviations. Negative standardized values indicate faster-than-average performances, while positive values indicate slower-than-average performances. This transformation allows us to compare relative performance across different events using a common scale.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  group_by(sport_name, event_name, gender) %>%
  mutate(standardized_time = as.vector(scale(time_seconds))) %>%
  ungroup()
```

#### Miscellaneous Variable Cleanup

The variable `event_type` could be very valuable for the stated goal of RQ3 in terms of the stakes of the race (prelims, finals, championship, etc.), but there are many missing values. Furthermore, when investigating unique event types, there are some typos and slight differences between names that cause the same event type to be essentially duplicated. To clean this variable, we first standardized existing names. Typos were addressed, and synonyms were combined into a single event type; "A" and "B" races were combined regardless of gender since a gender variable already exists to differentiate between them. 

We were also able to fill in some missing values based on existing knowledge of the sport. For instance, all cross country races are one-time races (no prelims and finals), and it is reasonable to assume that the races not marked as a "regional" or "national" are simply regular season races. Thus, these entries were filled in as "Regular Season". Track entries with missing event types were left alone as it is much more difficult to simply guess those event types. Again, it is not in the best interest of our analysis to omit entries with missing values for this variable as they still contain valid, important information elsewhere. 27 unique event types remained after this step.

```{r include=FALSE}
# Investigate messy event_type variable
# only_run %>%
  # count(event_type, sort = TRUE)

# unique(only_run$event_type)

only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(event_type = case_when(
    event_type %in% c("Final", "Finals", "FInals") ~ "Finals",
    event_type %in% c("Prelims", "Pelims", "1st Round",
                      "Round 1", "Qualifying") ~ "Prelims",
    event_type %in% c("Invite", "Invitational") ~ "Invitational",
    event_type %in% c("FR/SO", "Freshman/Sophmore",
                      "Freshman/Sophomore") ~ "Freshman/Sophomore",
    event_type %in% c("JR/SR/GRAD", "Junior/Senior/Grad") ~ "Junior/Senior/Grad",
    event_type %in% c("A Race", "Men A", "Women A",
                      "Men's A Race", "Women's A Race") ~ "A Race",
    event_type %in% c("B Race", "Men B", "Women B",
                      "Men's B Race", "Women's B Race") ~ "B Race",
    event_type == "" & regionals == FALSE & nationals == FALSE &
  sport_name == "Cross Country" ~ "Regular Season",
    TRUE ~ event_type
  ))

length(unique(only_run$event_type))
```

For the variable `event_name`, there are a number of non-standard running events that have minimal numbers of entries. For instance, 7000m is a non-standard cross country distance with only two recorded entries in the dataset. It was defined, based our existing knowledge of the running sports in this dataset, that a "niche" event was one with 200 or less observations. For cleanest data and to compare performances across standardized times, we filtered these out.

Prior to filtering, the dataset contained 33 unique race events. After removing non-standard and niche events with fewer than 200 total entries, 19 unique events remain with a relatively small amount of data loss (~1000 entries).

```{r include=FALSE}
# Investigate niche events
event_summary = only_run %>%
  count(sport_name, event_name, name = "count") %>%
  filter(count < 200) %>%
  arrange(count)

event_summary

# Filter out low-entry events
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(event_name = as.character(event_name)) %>% 
  group_by(event_name) %>%
  filter(n() >= 200) %>%  
  ungroup()

length(unique(only_run$event_name))
dim(only_run)
```

After creating the column `time_seconds` as a conversion of `result_time`, it was realized that some result times may have been entered incorrectly due to being extremely low for the event. The sport and event areas where these occurred were examined, and 29 seemingly incorrect entries were cleaned out using the world record times as a threshold.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  filter(
    !(sport_name == "Cross Country" & event_name == "8000m" &
        gender == "M" & time_seconds < 1320),
    !(sport_name == "Cross Country" & event_name == "6000m" &
        gender == "F" & time_seconds < 1080)
  )

dim(only_run)
```

#### Distance Classification

To facilitate comparisons across different race lengths, we created two additional variables: `distance_m` and `distance_category`. The variable `distance_m` represents event distances in meters, while `distance_category` groups events into short-, middle-, and long-distance races. Events of 400 meters or shorter were classified as short distance, events from 800 through 1500 meters were classified as middle distance, and events longer than 1500 meters were classified as long distance. These classifications allow us to investigate whether the relationships between race conditions and performance differ across race lengths while maintaining a consistent dataset for all three research questions.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    distance_m = case_when(
      event_name == "10 Mile" ~ 16093.44,
      event_name == "Half Marathon" ~ 21097.5,
      event_name == "Marathon" ~ 42195,
      event_name == "Mile" ~ 1609.344,
      str_detect(event_name, "^\\d+m$") ~
        as.numeric(str_remove(event_name, "m$")),
       ),
    distance_category = case_when(
      distance_m <= 400 ~ "Short Distance",
      distance_m <= 1500 ~ "Middle Distance",
      distance_m > 1500 ~ "Long Distance",
      ))
```

#### Weather Variable Classifications

To facilitate comparisons across different race conditions, we created categorical variables for temperature, humidity, and race stakes. Temperature measurements were grouped into cold, cool, mild, and hot conditions, while humidity was classified as low, moderate, or high. These categories simplify the interpretation of weather conditions while preserving the original numerical measurements for more detailed analysis. We also created a race classification variable using the existing national, regional, and NIRCA-only indicators. This allows us to compare performances across different levels of competition. All new variables were added to the shared cleaned dataset so they could be used consistently across the three research questions.

```{r include=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    temperature_category = case_when(
      temperature < 40 ~ "Cold",
      temperature < 60 ~ "Cool",
      temperature < 75 ~ "Mild",
      temperature >= 75 ~ "Hot",
      ),
    humidity_category = case_when(
      humidity < 40 ~ "Low",
      humidity < 70 ~ "Moderate",
      humidity >= 70 ~ "High",
      ))
only_run %>% count(temperature_category)
only_run %>% count(humidity_category)

```

```{r include=FALSE}
weather_run = only_run %>%
  filter(
    sport_name %in% c("Cross Country", "Outdoor Track"),
    !is.na(temperature),
    !is.na(humidity),
    !is.na(wind_speed),
    !is.na(standardized_time),
    !is.na(distance_category))

weather_run %>%
  summarise(
    results = n(),
    meets = n_distinct(meet_id))
```



### 3.2 Data Summary

The numerous variables in the NRCD dataset can be grouped based on shared characteristics and for ease of exploring research questions later. Groupings include race stakes, sports/events, results, altitude/elevation, weather, location, team, and gender.

"Race Stakes" variables, are variables that define the context of a meet. This could be classifying the race as club-only (`nirca_only`), regionals (`regionals`), or nationals (`nationals`), which are typically end-of-season championship meets. Furthermore, the variable `event_type` breaks it down with even further context, especially for track events when there may be preliminary and final rounds. The variables `nirca_only`, `regionals`, and `nationals` are each logical/Boolean vectors denoting the race classification.

Table 1 below displays the counts of entries under each classification and the total percent that each make up in the larger dataset. This table is designed to show the overlap that occurs between classifications - for instance, all regional and national meets are also classified as NIRCA (club) running meets only. There are some NIRCA-only regular season meets as well as meets that fall outside the NIRCA designation (could be NCAA, road races, etc.)

```{r echo=FALSE}
only_run = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    regionals = as.logical(regionals),
    nationals = as.logical(nationals),
    nirca_only = as.logical(nirca_only)
  )

stakes_summary = only_run %>%
  count(regionals, nationals, nirca_only, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(percentage = count / sum(count) * 100)

kable(
  stakes_summary,
  caption = "Number of Results in Each Race Stakes Classification"
)
```

Table 1 above reveals there are four combinations of race classification: NIRCA-only (regular season), NIRCA regionals, NIRCA nationals, and non-NIRCA (races not governed by NIRCA, which can include NCAA and other road races). To best visualize this, Figure 1 below shows the proportion of race entries categorized by each meet stakes combination. Regular season NIRCA competitions account for the largest share of entries, followed by NIRCA Nationals, non-NIRCA open meets, and NIRCA Regionals.

```{r echo=FALSE}
stakes_summary_class = stakes_summary %>%
  mutate(
    stake_category = case_when(
      !regionals & !nationals & !nirca_only ~ "Open / Non-NIRCA Meets",
      !regionals & !nationals & nirca_only  ~ "NIRCA Regular Season",
      !regionals & nationals & nirca_only   ~ "NIRCA Nationals",
      regionals & !nationals & nirca_only   ~ "NIRCA Regionals"
    )
  )

ggplot(stakes_summary_class, aes(x = reorder(stake_category, percentage), y = percentage)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 1: Distribution of Race Data by Stakes Classification",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percentage of Total Entries (%)"
  )
```

For the "Sports and Events" variables, `sport_name` shows four unique running sports represented in the dataset: Outdoor Track, Indoor Track, Cross Country, and Road Race. Each of these sports are assigned a number from 1-4 according to the `sport_id` variable. From these sports, each contain a collection of events that can be run in said sport given by the `event_name` variable. There are 19 unique events, each also associated with a number in the `event_id` variable. Some of these events can be ran in the different sports: for instance, the 800m can be ran both inside and outside on a track. 
Each sport has a unique number of events - cross country and road races have much less variety in race distances compared to track. Due to this and the large number of events particularly in track, vectors of the most common events for each sport were defined for upcoming summaries. The criteria for "most common" was defined as follows: events in cross country, indoor track, or outdoor had to have at least 1000 observations, while events in road races had to have at least 250 observations. These suitably encompassed the major race distances in each sport to provide the strongest summary. Figure 2 below shows this exact distribution of most common events by running sport.

```{r include=FALSE}
xc_events = c("8000m", "6000m", "5000m")

indoor_events = c("60m", "200m", "400m", "800m", "Mile", "3000m")

outdoor_events = c("100m", "200m", "400m", "800m", "1500m", "5000m")
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
event_summary = only_run %>%
  count(sport_name, event_name, name = "count") %>%
  filter(
    (sport_name == "Cross Country" & event_name %in% xc_events) |
    (sport_name == "Indoor Track" & event_name %in% indoor_events) |
    (sport_name == "Outdoor Track" & event_name %in% outdoor_events)
  )

ggplot(event_summary, aes(x = count, y = reorder_within(event_name, count, sport_name))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_reordered() +
  facet_wrap(~sport_name, scales = "free", nrow = 2, ncol = 2) + 
  labs(
    title = "Figure 2: Distribution of Most Common Running Events by Sport",
    x = "Number of Results",
    y = "Running Event"
  )
```

Crucial to our analysis are the time performances of the athletes. The variable `result_time` gives us these times, and they were converted into the lowest unit `time_seconds` for ease of comparison during the cleaning process. Result times are most directly associated with the event being ran and gender. Due to the differences in variety of events per sport, custom summaries per sport are given below.

Figure 3 displays distribution of cross country times across the 8000m, 6000m, and 5000m distances. Men typically only run the 8000m, while there is data for both men and women in the 6000m and 5000m.

```{r echo=FALSE}
xc = only_run %>%
  filter(sport_name == "Cross Country", event_name %in% xc_events) %>%
  mutate(time_minutes = time_seconds / 60)
  

ggplot(xc, aes(x = time_minutes, y = event_name, fill = gender)) +
  geom_violin() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 3: Time Distributions by Cross Country Event",
    x = "Result Time (Minutes)",
    y = NULL
  )

```

The track events are much more numerous, so average and median times for the most common events are provided in Tables 2 and 3 below.

```{r include=FALSE}
indoor_summary = only_run %>%
  filter(sport_name == "Indoor Track",
         event_name %in% indoor_events) %>%
  group_by(event_name, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_time = round(mean(time_seconds), 2),
    median_time = round(median(time_seconds), 2),
  ) %>%
  arrange(mean_time)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
kable(indoor_summary, col.names = c("Event", "Gender", "Mean Time (Seconds)", "Median Time (Seconds)"), caption = "Average and Median Times for Indoor Track Events")
```

```{r include=FALSE}
outdoor_summary = only_run %>%

         event_name %in% outdoor_events) %>%
```

To better understand the environmental conditions represented in our dataset, we examined the distributions of temperature, humidity, and wind speed. These variables were selected because they have relatively complete data compared to other weather measurements. The following summaries use outdoor running results with recorded weather measurements, allowing us to describe the conditions under which athletes competed. We calculated descriptive statistics and examined the distribution of temperatures to identify typical race conditions and the extent to which extreme weather is represented.

```{r include=FALSE}
weather_summary = data.frame(
  Variable = c("Temperature", "Humidity", "Wind Speed"),
  Mean = sapply(weather_run[c("temperature", "humidity", "wind_speed")], mean),
  SD = sapply(weather_run[c("temperature", "humidity", "wind_speed")], sd),
  Min = sapply(weather_run[c("temperature", "humidity", "wind_speed")], min),
  Median = sapply(weather_run[c("temperature", "humidity", "wind_speed")], median),
  Max = sapply(weather_run[c("temperature", "humidity", "wind_speed")], max)
)
```

These calculations showed that the outdoor races in our weather-analysis dataset occurred under a wide range of environmental conditions. The average temperature was 57.85°F, with recorded temperatures ranging from 30.15°F to 93.61°F. Relative humidity averaged 63.55%, ranging from 24% to 100%, while wind speed averaged 8.59, with values ranging from 0 to 23.02. These differences indicate that our dataset includes a variety of weather conditions, providing an opportunity to investigate how temperature, humidity, and wind speed relate to running performance across different race distances.

To further examine the weather conditions represented in our dataset, we created a histogram showing the distribution of recorded race temperatures. This visualization allows us to identify the most common temperature ranges and evaluate how well unusually hot or cold conditions are represented.


```{r echo=FALSE}
ggplot(weather_run, aes(x = temperature)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "gray", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Number of Race Results", title = "Figure 4: Distribution of Race Observations Across Temperature Groups")
```


The distribution of race temperatures is concentrated primarily between 45°F and 75°F, with the highest frequency occurring around 60°F. Temperatures become less common toward both extremes, particularly above 80°F. This indicates that most recorded performances occurred under relatively moderate temperatures, while unusually hot conditions are less represented. The uneven distribution of observations across temperatures is important to consider when interpreting performance trends, as estimates at extreme temperatures may be less reliable due to smaller sample sizes.

For the "Altitude and Elevation" variables, we have `altitude`, `elevation_gain`, and `elevation_loss`. Each of these give us a further understanding of some of the conditions of the location the runners are competing at. For each of those variables, here we feature simple statistics for each in the overall dataset, as well as histograms providing further visualization of each variable. We know as a result of this information that we should be able to find them statistically significant for our research questions.

```{r include=FALSE}
    gain_sd = sd(elevation_gain, na.rm = TRUE),
    gain_min = min(elevation_gain, na.rm = TRUE),
    gain_max = max(elevation_gain, na.rm= TRUE),
    
    loss_mean = mean(elevation_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_median = median(elevation_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_sd = sd(elevation_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_min = min(elevation_loss, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_max = max(elevation_loss, na.rm= TRUE)
  )
```

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(only_run, aes(x = altitude)) +
```

### 3.3 Research Question Exploration

### RQ1: Weather Conditions and Running Performance

Our first research question examines whether temperature, humidity, and wind speed are associated with differences in running performance across race distances. Using outdoor race results with available weather measurements, we compared average standardized finishing times across short-, middle-, and long-distance events. Because times were standardized within each combination of sport, event, and gender, negative values indicate faster-than-average performances, while positive values indicate slower-than-average performances.

To visualize these relationships, weather measurements were grouped into five-degree temperature intervals, five-percentage-point humidity intervals, and two-unit wind-speed intervals. Each plotted point represents the average standardized time of results within a weather interval and distance category. We excluded intervals containing fewer than 30 valid results to reduce the influence of very small samples. However, because multiple results can originate from the same meet, the number of individual observations does not necessarily reflect the number of independent weather environments represented.

##### Temperature and Running Performance

We first examined the relationship between temperature and standardized race time across the three distance categories. Because higher standardized values indicate slower performances relative to the event average, an upward trend would suggest an association between warmer temperatures and slower race times. Comparing the three distance categories allows us to explore whether this relationship differs by race length.


```{r echo=FALSE}
temp_summary = weather_run %>%
  mutate(temp_group = floor(temperature / 5) * 5) %>%
  group_by(distance_category, temp_group) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_time = mean(standardized_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 30)

ggplot(temp_summary, aes(x = temp_group, y = avg_time)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~distance_category) +
  labs(x = "Temperature (°F)", y = "Average Standardized Race Time", title = "Figure 11: Standardized Race Time by Temperature Group")
```


The relationship between temperature and standardized performance appears to vary across race distances. Long-distance events show a generally increasing trend in standardized times at warmer temperatures, suggesting that higher temperatures may be associated with slower relative performances. However, this relationship is not consistent across all intervals. Short-distance performances fluctuate around zero without a clear overall trend. Middle-distance results show a particularly large positive spike near 67.5°F, indicating substantially slower-than-average performances within that interval. This unusual value warrants further investigation to determine whether it reflects a broader weather-related pattern or results from a small number of meets.

##### Humidity and Running Performance

Next, we examined whether relative humidity is associated with standardized race times. Higher humidity can influence the body's ability to dissipate heat, potentially affecting performance during prolonged exercise. By comparing the three distance categories, we aim to identify whether longer races exhibit different patterns from shorter events as humidity increases.

```{r echo=FALSE}
humidity_summary = weather_run %>%
  mutate(humidity_group = floor(humidity / 5) * 5) %>%
  group_by(distance_category, humidity_group) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_time = mean(standardized_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 30)

ggplot(humidity_summary, aes(x = humidity_group, y = avg_time)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~distance_category) +
  labs(x = "Relative Humidity (%)", y = "Average Standardized Race Time", title = "Figure 12: Standardized Race Time by Relative Humidity")
```

The relationship between humidity and standardized race time differs across distance categories. Long-distance performances remain relatively close to the event average across most humidity intervals, with somewhat higher standardized times at the highest humidity levels. Middle-distance results show a pronounced positive spike near 32.5% humidity, followed by substantially lower standardized times at higher humidity levels. Short-distance results also exhibit an unusually high average standardized time near 32.5% humidity, while most other intervals remain close to or below zero. These patterns do not suggest a consistent relationship between increasing humidity and slower performance, but they identify several unusual intervals that may be influenced by individual meets.

##### Wind Speed and Running Performance

Finally, we examined the relationship between wind speed and standardized race time. Unlike temperature and humidity, the influence of wind may depend heavily on its direction relative to the runner, as headwinds and tailwinds can have different effects on performance. Although our analysis uses wind speed rather than runner-relative wind direction, the visualization provides an initial opportunity to examine whether performance patterns vary across race distances as wind speed changes.

```{r echo=FALSE}
wind_summary = weather_run %>%
  mutate(wind_group = floor(wind_speed / 2) * 2) %>%
  group_by(distance_category, wind_group) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_time = mean(standardized_time, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 30)

ggplot(wind_summary, aes(x = wind_group, y = avg_time)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~distance_category) +
  labs(x = "Wind Speed (MPH)", y = "Average Standardized Race Time", title = "Figure 13: Standardized Race Time by Wind Speed")
```

Wind speed shows different patterns across the three distance categories. Long-distance events exhibit a generally decreasing trend in standardized race times as wind speed increases, suggesting that higher recorded wind speeds are associated with faster relative performances in this sample. However, this pattern is irregular and does not necessarily indicate that wind improves performance. Middle-distance events show unusually high standardized times at very low wind speeds, followed by values closer to zero as wind speed increases. Short-distance events display a similar positive spike at low wind speeds, while most remaining intervals fluctuate around or below zero. Because wind direction relative to runners is not accounted for, and several unusual values occur within specific intervals, these findings should be interpreted cautiously.

##### Investigation of Unusual Weather-Performance Patterns

After examining the three weather-performance visualizations, we investigated selected intervals with unusually high or low average standardized times. Because multiple athletes may compete at the same meet under similar environmental conditions, we examined both the number of individual race results and the number of distinct meets contributing to these intervals. This helps determine whether unusual patterns are supported by multiple competitions or are concentrated within a single meet.

Further investigation revealed that several unusual spikes in our weather-performance visualizations were concentrated within individual meets. Of the eight intervals examined, three contained results from only one meet. Most notably, the middle-distance spikes observed at temperatures of 65–70°F, humidity levels of 30–35%, and wind speeds of 0–2 each contained 46 race results from a single meet, with an identical average standardized time of 1.208. This strongly suggests that the same competition may be responsible for all three unusual patterns rather than three separate weather-related effects.

Other intervals also showed substantial concentration within individual meets. For example, the short-distance wind-speed interval of 2–4 contained 33 results from one meet, while 95.2% of the 580 long-distance results in the 20–22 wind-speed interval came from a single competition. In contrast, the long-distance humidity interval of 95–100% included 585 results across 10 meets, with no individual meet contributing more than 26.2% of observations. These findings demonstrate that the number of race results alone does not necessarily indicate how broadly a pattern is represented across competitions. Because athletes competing at the same meet may share weather conditions and other race characteristics, apparent relationships should be interpreted cautiously, particularly when observations are concentrated within a small number of meets.

### RQ2: Altitude, Elevation, and Team Location Exploration

For starters, we had some outliers on standardized time that were over 5 standard deviations away, causing the graphs to look messy and unreadable. We agreed that was too high, and there were only ~200 of those out of the other thousands of rows. We removed those with more than five standard deviations.

```{r include=FALSE}
outliers_5 = only_run %>%
  filter(abs(standardized_time) > 5) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(standardized_time))) %>%
  select(
    sport_name,
    event_name,
    gender,
    result_time,
    time_seconds,
    standardized_time,
    altitude, 
    team_name,
    meet_name
  )

outliers_5

nrow(outliers_5)

outliers_5 %>%
  arrange(desc(time_seconds))

outliers_5 %>%
  count(sport_name, event_name, gender, sort = TRUE)

outliers_5 %>%
  arrange(desc(altitude)) %>%
  select(meet_name, team_name, altitude, standardized_time)

only_run <- only_run %>%
  filter(
    is.na(standardized_time) |
      abs(standardized_time) <= 5
  )
```

As we explore the different effects of certain contexts on race, some of the most important are the location and altitude of the race itself. Depending on where certain races are held around the country, runners are likely to find individual differences among them, specifically related to altitude and sometimes elevation. Either way, we want to determine how much altitude and race location themselves are effecting the runner's performances. We determined it'd be best to split altitudes into four categories: Low, Moderate, High, and Very High, in order to more easily visualize the altitude data.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
only_run %>%
  mutate(
    altitude_category = case_when(
      altitude < 1000 ~ "Low",
      altitude < 3000 ~ "Moderate",
      altitude < 5000 ~ "High",
      altitude >= 5000 ~ "Very High",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
    
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(altitude_category), !is.na(standardized_time)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = altitude_category, y = standardized_time)) + 
  geom_boxplot() + 
  labs( 
    title = "Figure 14: Athlete Performance Across Race Altitude", 
    x = "Race Altitude Category", 
    y = "Standardized Time" 
  )
```

We can see based off this box plot that the median indicates that moderate level of altitudes find an average standardization score of 0, which is about an average score in this set of race times. For both High and Low altitudes, we can see that the median hovers around -0.1 or -0.2 for both, indicating that runners tend to score slightly above average in those altitudes. For Very High altitudes, we see a median of about -0.5, which is significantly above the average score. Therefore, we can conclude that altitude of the, for the most part, is not super significant for race times aside from those with Very High altitudes.

We also can look at elevation gain and elevation loss. We don't have nearly as much data on this as altitude, but still is good to understand how, if at all, the elevation gain and elevation loss is effecting the runner's performances.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
ggplot(
  only_run %>%
    filter(!is.na(elevation_gain), !is.na(standardized_time)),
  aes(x = elevation_gain, y = standardized_time)
) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 15: Standardized Race Performance vs. Elevation Gain",
    x = "Race Elevation Gain",
    y = "Standardized Time"
  )

ggplot(
  only_run %>%
    filter(!is.na(elevation_loss), !is.na(standardized_time)),
  aes(x = elevation_loss, y = standardized_time)
) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 16: Standardized Race Performance vs. Elevation Loss",
    x = "Race Elevation Loss",
    y = "Standardized Time"
  )
```

We can clearly see in these scatter plots that elevation gain and loss, respectively, have a positive, yet very weak correlation. We can conclude that the two variables attached with standardized scores have some tendency to increase together, but the relationship is not very reliable due to it being very weak in nature. The results from this graph, as well as the lack of amount of elevation gain and loss data in the data set, may likely reasonably lead us to take out elevation from the analysis for runner performance.

We also can investigate the performances of athletes based on the team location. Due to the large number of teams, we start of by looking at the top 15 teams with the most participants and see their results.

```{r echo=FALSE}
team_counts = only_run %>%
  group_by(team_name) %>%
  summarise(
    total_races = n()
  )

top_15_teams = team_counts %>%
  slice_max(order_by = total_races, n = 15)

top_15_data = only_run %>%
  filter(team_name %in% top_15_teams$team_name)

ggplot(top_15_data, aes(x = team_name, y = standardized_time)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 17: Athelete Performance Across Team Locations",
    x = "Team",
    y = "Standardized Time"
  )
```

We see in this box plot graph that most of the schools in the top 15 participation had a median time slightly less than 0. This indicates to us that many of the top schools and their location prepared their athletes well in most cases. Many of these schools are well-known for their athletics, so we can reasonably understand that it makes sense that they're going to be slightly above average in run times. As we go further into analysis, we can determine how potentially the altitudes and locations of these schools themselves allow the runners to be better prepared for certain altitude races around the country based upon that. For example, a east coast state, like Maryland, is going to have significantly lower altitude than a state like Colorado, where it is high. 

### RQ3: Exploring Race Context through Classifications and Characteristics

When exploring race context, it is imperative to examine the stakes of the races. Everything from time in the season to the race classification can have a physical and/or mental impact on athletes, ultimately influencing how well they perform. Naturally, the first place to start when analyzing race stakes is the season progression - that is, how the performances of athletes change over the course of the season. The importance of races tends to go up as the season progresses, especially as regular season transitions into championship season.

The first visuals below explore progressions across the season for major events within the sports. These visuals use raw result times since each season occurs across a different span of months. Cross country occurs during the months of August-November, though a majority of meets occur between September and October. Figure 18 averages times for each month across all years of data, which spans 2003-2025.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
xc_monthly = only_run %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Cross Country", 
    event_name %in% xc_events, 
    !(event_name == "6000m" & gender == "M")) %>%
  mutate(month = month(date)) %>%
  group_by(month, event_name, gender) %>%
  summarise(mean_time = mean(time_seconds) / 60)
  
ggplot(xc_monthly, aes(x = month, y = mean_time, color = gender, group = gender)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~event_name) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 18: Average Cross Country Performances by Month (2003-2025)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Race Time (Minutes)",
    color = "Gender"
  )
```

The same visuals were generated for the sport of track. These visuals display a variety of events spanning a wider range of distances, from short sprints to long distances. Indoor track typically occurs during the months of December-March, and average seasonal progressions across recorded years 2008-2026 are displayed below in Figure 19.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
indoor_monthly = only_run %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Indoor Track",
    event_name %in% indoor_events
  ) %>%
  mutate(month = factor(month(date), levels = c(12, 1, 2, 3))) %>%
  group_by(month, event_name, gender) %>%
  summarise(mean_time = mean(time_seconds)) %>%
  mutate(event_name = factor(event_name, levels = indoor_events))


ggplot(indoor_monthly, aes(x = month, y = mean_time, color = gender, group = gender)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~event_name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 19: Average Indoor Track Performances by Month (2008-2026)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Race Time (Seconds)",
    color = "Gender"
  )
```

The same visual was generated in Figure 20 for outdoor track. The types of events are slightly different but still span events from short sprints to long distances. Outdoor track typically runs from spring to summer months, which is reflected below.

```{r echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
outdoor_monthly = only_run %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Outdoor Track",
    event_name %in% outdoor_events
  ) %>%
  mutate(month = month(date)) %>%
  group_by(month, event_name, gender) %>%
  summarise(mean_time = mean(time_seconds)) %>%
  mutate(event_name = factor(event_name, levels = outdoor_events))


ggplot(outdoor_monthly, aes(x = month, y = mean_time, color = gender, group = gender)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~event_name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 20: Average Outdoor Track Performances by Month (2004-2026)",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Average Race Time (Seconds)",
    color = "Gender"
  )
```

The next step in exploring potential effects of race stakes is looking at performances across the different race classifications. Figure 21 maps out the distributions of performances across the two major events in cross country according to the race classifications of "Regular", "Regionals", and "Nationals". All of these classifications fall under the NIRCA umbrella - that is, all of the represented performances came from club-only meets.

```{r echo=FALSE}
xc_stakes = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    stake_category = case_when(
      !regionals & !nationals & !nirca_only ~ "Open / Non-NIRCA Meets",
      !regionals & !nationals & nirca_only  ~ "Regular",
      !regionals & nationals & nirca_only   ~ "Nationals",
      regionals & !nationals & nirca_only   ~ "Regionals"
    )) %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Cross Country",
    event_name %in% xc_events & event_name != '5000m',
    stake_category != "Open / Non-NIRCA Meets",
    !(event_name == "6000m" & gender == "M")
    ) %>%
  mutate(stake_category = factor(
    stake_category,
    levels = c("Regular","Regionals","Nationals"))
    )

ggplot(xc_stakes, aes(x = stake_category, y = time_seconds / 60)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(
    ~event_name,
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = as_labeller(c("6000m" = "6000m Women", "8000m" = "8000m Men"))) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 21: Cross Country Performance by Race Stakes",
    x = "Race Stakes",
    y = "Race Time (Minutes)",
  )
```

A similar visualization was developed in Figure 22 for track; due to the volume of events, certain events from across the spectrum of distances were chosen to best represent the range of distances in the sport. This includes a short sprint (100m), a long sprint (400m), and a middle distance (1500m). Furthermore, the "regionals" classification does not exist for track, so only performances in regular season vs. championship meets could be compared here.

```{r echo=FALSE}
sprint_stakes = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    stake_category = case_when(
      !regionals & !nationals & !nirca_only ~ "Open / Non-NIRCA Meets",
      !regionals & !nationals & nirca_only  ~ "Regular",
      !regionals & nationals & nirca_only   ~ "Nationals",
      regionals & !nationals & nirca_only   ~ "Regionals",
    )) %>%
  mutate(event_name = factor(event_name, levels = c("100m", "400m", "1500m"))) %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Outdoor Track",
    event_name %in% c('100m', "400m", "1500m"),
    stake_category != ("Open / Non-NIRCA Meets"),
    ) %>%
  mutate(stake_category = factor(
    stake_category,
    levels = c("Regular", "Nationals"))
    )

ggplot(sprint_stakes, aes(x = stake_category, y = time_seconds)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(
    ~event_name,
    scales = "free_y",
    ) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 22: Track Performance by Race Stakes",
    x = "Race Stakes",
    y = "Race Time (Seconds)",
  )
```

In exploring race stakes, it is also necessary to compare performance distributions between NIRCA and non-NIRCA races. NIRCA races include club-only amateur collegiate athletes, while non-NIRCA races can be hosted by other governing bodies such as the NCAA. This means that, in non-NIRCA races, amateur athletes may be competing against high-level NCAA athletes. Among the two major races in the sport of cross country, performance distributions are compared between NIRCA and non-NIRCA races in Figure 23.

```{r echo=FALSE}
xc_nirca = only_run %>%
  mutate(
    competition_type = case_when(
      !regionals & !nationals & !nirca_only ~ "Non-NIRCA",
      !regionals & !nationals & nirca_only ~ "NIRCA"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    sport_name == "Cross Country",
    event_name %in% c("6000m", "8000m"),
    !is.na(competition_type),
    !(event_name == "6000m" & gender == "M")
  )

ggplot(xc_nirca, aes(x = competition_type, y = time_seconds / 60)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~event_name, scales = "free_y", labeller = as_labeller(c("6000m" = "6000m Women", "8000m" = "8000m Men"))) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 23: Cross Country Performance at NIRCA vs. Non-NIRCA Meets",
    x = "Competition Type",
    y = "Race Time (Minutes)"
  )
```



### 3.4 Qualitative Analysis

### RQ1: Weather Conditions and Running Performance

Our preliminary analysis suggests that the relationships between weather conditions and running performance may differ across race distances, although no consistent pattern emerged across all three weather variables. Long-distance events generally showed higher standardized race times at warmer temperatures, suggesting an association between increasing temperature and slower relative performance. However, short-distance results fluctuated without a clear temperature-related trend, while middle-distance events exhibited several unusually large spikes. Humidity and wind speed also showed varying relationships across distance categories, but neither demonstrated a consistent association with slower performance as conditions increased.

Further investigation revealed that several of the most pronounced patterns were heavily influenced by individual meets. In particular, the middle-distance spikes for temperature, humidity, and wind speed each contained 46 race results from a single meet, with an identical average standardized time of 1.208. Additionally, 95.2% of the 580 long-distance results in the 20–22 wind-speed interval came from one meet. These findings suggest that some apparent weather-related patterns may reflect characteristics of specific competitions rather than broader relationships between weather and performance.

Overall, our findings provide preliminary evidence that weather conditions may be associated with running performance differently across race distances, but the strength and direction of these relationships remain uncertain. In our final analysis, we plan to investigate these relationships more systematically while accounting for differences between meets and other factors that may influence race times. This will help us determine whether the patterns observed in our exploratory visualizations persist after considering potential confounding variables.

### RQ2: Altitude, Elevation, and Team Location Exploration

In our initial analysis of altitude, elevation, and location, we find that at least two of these are significant for our research in this data set. Elevation gain and loss, though ideally important for effecting race times, does not have a large amount of this data in this particular set, with about 23,000 for each out of the 187,000 in the original set. On top of that, we can see in the graphs that there is a positive but very weak relationship between the data points. Thus, this information does not seem to reveal much significance for the race times we have been provided.

Altitude, however, appears to have more significance to the race times. We see that the runners times for "Low" and "High" altitudes, we find that the runners are slightly above average in their race times, at a median -0.1 and -0.2, respectively. We see that at "Moderate" altitudes that racers run at about average in their race times, with the median reaches 0. Based on the context of training and race locations at a general level, moderate altitude of just over 3000 is slightly above the average altitude in the country, and thus the standardized time at 0 seems reasonable for that altitude level. We also can see that those who ran at a "High" altitude in races had an average standardized score of -0.5, which is significantly above average. The main caveat there is that there not nearly as many locations with that high of an altitude, and so the samples are not as strong as the other three.

When it comes to locations of the athletes' teams, we can initially look at the schools with the top 15 participation in races in the data set. All of the schools had at least a median score of 0 or less, indicating that they're at least average or above average in terms of race times. Future analysis will allow us more in depth breakdown of each team's training locations and how those altitudes might help or hurt them in their preparation for certain different altitudes at different races. Overall, it's very clear that the locations the runners are coming from most certainly do have an effect on how they perform at different races. 

### RQ3: Exploring Race Context through Classifications and Characteristics

It is crucial to understand both the circumstances surrounding race day as well as the characteristics inherent to a race. These characteristics include the type and classification of a race, which can have differing physical and mental impacts on athletes depending on the sport and event. The time in the season of which a race occurs will also inherently have an impact - races gain increased importance as the season wears on, and theoretically, athletes will strive to improve as a result. In the data visualizations for our third research question, we sought to identify trends that may indicate correlations between race stakes and athlete performance. Specifically, one might hypothesize that the greater the stakes, the faster the times.

Figures 18, 19, and 20 display performance progressions across the seasons of each running sport represented in the data set. Across the months of cross country, there are clear declines in times as the season wears on with only a couple of exceptions. This would establish a correlation between improved performance and late-season races, though it should be stressed that time of season is just one of many considerations when determining why athletes perform the way they do. The same cannot be said of indoor track, where average result times experience an upward trend as the season wears on. Exceptions to this include the longer-distance events. This potentially indicates that it is harder to improve in the short distances even as the season progresses, perhaps simply due to the smaller distance and thus smaller margin for improvement. However, the long distance race performances experience a flat-to-downward trend, reflecting an increased margin for improvement. This is an intriguing finding in the long distances, as athletes tend to experience more burnout in these events as the season wears on. However, it seems that the increased margin for improvement wins out.

Outdoor track events show declines in times across the board – this indicates that athletes generally continue to improve as the outdoor season progresses, regardless of race distance. This trend may reflect both the cumulative effects of training throughout the academic year as well as the gradual increase in meet importance. The smaller, more controlled environment of an indoor track race may also explain the relative lack of improvement in indoor track. These patterns suggest that the relationship between time of season and athletic performance varies between running sports and even between events within the same sport. While late-season races generally appear to produce faster results in cross country and outdoor track, indoor track demonstrates a more complicated relationship, particularly among shorter-distance events.

When comparing performances across race classifications in both Figures 21 and 22, there are visible declines in the average times and distribution centers from regular season races to national races. There is a clear correlation between faster times and heightened race stakes - championship performances not only tend to have faster times, but the distributions are more compact with less outliers, indicating the athletes are attempting to run their best at some of the most important meets of the year. The mental effect of knowing it is a championship race may play a part in this clear showing of stronger performances, though cumulative training over time must again be accounted for when determining why performances are strong.

One final finding of note comes in the comparison of performance distributions between NIRCA and non-NIRCA races. Non-NIRCA races have lower average times and much more compact distributions compared to NIRCA races. Non-NIRCA races are often hosted by NCAA schools - amateur club athletes can compete in these races if no NIRCA race is available and nearby for them to participate in. Thus, it is possible to conclude that the presence of high-caliber athletes may push the club athletes represented in this dataset to perform better, potentially explaining the visibly lower, compact distributions in comparison with NIRCA-only races.
